title: DNS & HTTP Debugging Tools
summary: The application-layer counterparts to ping/traceroute — dig, curl, and browser DevTools — for debugging DNS and HTTP directly.

slides.markdown:
`dig`/`nslookup`, `curl`, and browser DevTools are the application-layer counterparts to ping/traceroute — instead of network reachability, they debug **DNS resolution** and **HTTP behavior** directly, which is where most real-world "the site is slow/broken" reports actually live.

- `dig` queries DNS servers directly and shows exactly what they answered.
- `curl` makes a manual HTTP request with full visibility into headers and timing.
- DevTools' Network tab visualizes the same phases graphically, request by request.

slides.subTitle: Querying DNS directly
slides.markdown:
```bash
dig example.com

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.  3600  IN  A  93.184.216.34
```

`dig` sends a DNS query and shows the raw response — the **ANSWER SECTION** matters most: record type (`A` for IPv4), value, and **TTL** (3600s — how long resolvers should cache it). `nslookup` does the same job, more tersely; `dig` is generally preferred for its parseable answer section. See [dns-resolution](dns-resolution).

slides.subTitle: dig +trace
slides.markdown:
```bash
dig +trace example.com
```

Instead of asking your resolver for the final answer, `+trace` walks the DNS hierarchy manually — root servers, then `.com` TLD servers, then `example.com`'s authoritative nameservers — showing each referral. This is the tool for diagnosing **propagation issues**: if you just changed nameservers or a record, `+trace` shows what the authoritative source says *right now*, bypassing any stale cached answer your resolver holds.

```bash
curl -v -w "\ntime_total: %{time_total}s\n" https://example.com
```

`-v` (verbose) shows the full request and response — headers, TLS negotiation, redirects followed. `-w` with format variables prints timing data curl already measured. Where DevTools requires a browser, `curl` gives the same visibility from any terminal — a server over SSH, a CI pipeline — making it the tool of choice when a GUI isn't available.

Response headers usually explain the confusing behavior, if you read them:

- **Caching** — `Cache-Control`, `Age`, `X-Cache: HIT/MISS` show whether a response came from cache and for how long.
- **CORS** — `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (present or absent) explains why a browser request was blocked when the same request via `curl` works fine (curl doesn't enforce CORS).
- **Redirects** — a `3xx` with `Location` shows exactly where a request ended up.

Most "why is this weird" questions have their answer in a header nobody looked at.

slides.subTitle: The request waterfall
slides.markdown:
![Browser DevTools Network tab showing a waterfall of requests, each with a colored timing breakdown bar](assets/devtools-network-waterfall.svg)

Every row is one request; the colored bar shows time spent in each phase. Reading the waterfall (which requests start when, which block others) is usually faster than digging through curl output one request at a time, especially for a page loading dozens of resources.

assets.alt: Browser DevTools Network tab showing a waterfall of requests, each with a colored timing breakdown bar

slides.markdown:
![A single request's waterfall bar broken into DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, waiting (TTFB), and content download](assets/devtools-waterfall-phases.svg)

Each segment is a different bottleneck with a different fix: slow **DNS** points at the resolver; slow **connect/TLS** points at network path or cert overhead; a long **TTFB** points at server processing; slow **download** points at payload size. See [client-server-request-lifecycle](client-server-request-lifecycle).

assets.alt: A single request's waterfall bar broken into DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, waiting (TTFB), and content download

slides.markdown:
| | curl | DevTools Network tab |
|---|---|---|
| Interface | Command line | Browser GUI |
| Best for | Scripting, headless environments, precise single-request inspection | Visual overview of a whole page load, many requests at once |
| Shows | Exact headers/timing for one request you construct | Every request the page actually made, as the browser made it |

**How to decide:** debugging one specific API call, especially from a script or server? `curl`. Debugging why a whole page feels slow, with dozens of requests and resources involved? DevTools' waterfall view.

slides.subTitle: "Slow" isn't one thing
slides.markdown:
A vague, common complaint: **"the API is slow."** That hides at least four different bottlenecks — DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, and server processing (TTFB) — each with a different fix. Blaming "the API" (server code) when the real delay is a slow DNS resolver, or a badly-configured TLS cert chain, sends debugging effort at the wrong layer.

Before optimizing, break "slow" down using the waterfall or curl's timing breakdown.
